question.problem:
Which of the following are orthogonal projection matrices?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{3}{4} & -\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{13} & \frac{6}{13} \\ \frac{6}{13} & \frac{4}{13}\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that $Q$ is an orthogonal projection matrix if and only if ${Q}^{2}=Q$ and ${Q}^{T}=Q.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- $A$ is *not* an orthogonal projection matrix. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\ne A.\end{aligned}
$$

- $B$ is *not* an orthogonal projection matrix. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{T}\ne B.\end{aligned}
$$

- $C$ is an orthogonal projection matrix. Indeed,
${C}^{T}=C$
and

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{2} & =C\cdot C \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{13} & \frac{6}{13} \\ \frac{6}{13} & \frac{4}{13}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{13} & \frac{6}{13} \\ \frac{6}{13} & \frac{4}{13}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{169}[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{169}[\begin{aligned}117 & 78 \\ 78 & 52\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{13} & \frac{6}{13} \\ \frac{6}{13} & \frac{4}{13}\end{aligned}] \\  & =C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$C$ only."
